```{r knitr-options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 92)
```

Work with an AI assistant unfolds as a conversation in which tasks are
delegated, plans are made, code is executed and inspected, results are
explained and errors are repaired. Coding the messages of such sessions
turns each session into a sequence of collaboration moves, and the order of
those moves describes how the collaboration proceeds: whether an
explanation leads to further investigation, what typically follows a
delegation, and which histories precede a repair.

Two analytical choices shape any sequence analysis of such data. The first is
how the log is cut into sequences. Collaboration logs are usually exported
as one row per message with a timestamp and a session identifier, and the
right unit of analysis is the session, not the calendar day or the project.
The second is the granularity of the state space. A coding scheme with eight
moves can be collapsed into three broader categories, and the two levels can
tell different stories about how much history matters.

This case study fits variable-order transition trees (Ron, Singer & Tishby,
1996; Bühlmann & Wyner, 1999) to a coded log of human-AI collaboration
sessions. It asks how the log should be reshaped into sequences, how the
coarse and fine state spaces differ in memory and predictability, which
histories predict which moves, and which histories precede a repair.

```{r setup}
library(transitiontrees)
```

## Data

`ai_long` is a bundled log of coded messages from AI-assisted project work,
one row per coded move. A message can carry several codes, so a message may
occupy several rows.

- **Actor:** `project` — the project; 34 projects contribute sessions.
- **Session:** `session_id` — the collaboration session, 428 in total; each
  session is one sequence.
- **Time:** `timestamp` — Unix time in seconds; `session_date` holds the same
  date as text.
- **Order:** `order_in_session` — the position of the move within its
  session; `message_id` and `code_order` identify the message and the
  position of the code within it.
- **Fine state:** `code` — the move, one of eight codes (`Ask`, `Delegate`,
  `Execute`, `Explain`, `Investigate`, `Plan`, `Repair`, `Report`).
- **Coarse state:** `cluster` — the category of the move: `Action`
  (`Delegate`, `Execute`, `Investigate`), `Communication` (`Ask`, `Explain`,
  `Report`) or `Repair` (`Plan`, `Repair`).

## From a message log to session sequences

The timestamp is stored as Unix seconds. Converting it to clock time shows
its resolution.

```{r timestamp}
with(ai_long, table(clock_time = format(as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"), "%H:%M:%S")))
with(ai_long, range(as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC")))
```

All 8551 timestamps carry the same clock time, 22:00 UTC, which is midnight
in a UTC+2 time zone: the timestamp records the date of the session
(`session_date`), not the time of the message. The log spans about a month
of sessions. A time-gap rule, which starts a
new session whenever two consecutive events are more than 15 minutes apart,
cannot recover sessions from such a timestamp. `prepare_input()` shows the
consequence: with `is_unix_time = TRUE` the numeric column is read as Unix
time, and every day of a project becomes one sequence.

```{r time-route}
prepare_input(ai_long, actor = "project", time = "timestamp",
              is_unix_time = TRUE, order = "order_in_session",
              action = "code") |>
  nrow()
```

The time-gap route produces 160 sequences, one per project and day, because
several sessions of the same project held on the same day are merged into
one. Naming the session column instead takes the sessions from the data,
and `order` orders the moves within each session.

```{r session-route}
sessions <- prepare_input(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                          order = "order_in_session", action = "code")
nrow(sessions)
summary(rowSums(!is.na(sessions)))
```

The session route gives the 428 sessions of the data. Sessions are short
and uneven: the median session holds 13 moves, the longest 138. The rest of
the analysis passes the same arguments to `context_tree()` and
`tune_tree()`, which reshape the log in the same way before fitting.

## Coarse and fine state spaces

The fine tree models the eight codes, the coarse tree the three categories.
Both are grown to a depth of three moves with at least ten occurrences per
context.

```{r fit}
fine <- context_tree(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                     order = "order_in_session", action = "code",
                     max_depth = 3L, min_count = 10L)
coarse <- context_tree(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                       order = "order_in_session", action = "cluster",
                       max_depth = 3L, min_count = 10L)
state_frequencies(fine)
state_frequencies(coarse)
```

`Execute` (38.1% of moves), `Investigate` (27.1%) and `Plan` (18.9%)
dominate the fine codes; `Ask` is the rarest move (1.2%). At the coarse
level, `Action` covers 68.6% of moves, `Repair` 22.0% and `Communication`
9.4%. Because `Plan` belongs to the `Repair` category, most coarse `Repair`
moves are planning moves; the code `Repair` itself accounts for 3.0% of
moves.

How much history each state space needs is a question for held-out data.
`tune_tree()` cross-validates depths from zero, the model with no history,
to three, with and without pruning, over five folds of sessions.

```{r tune-fine}
tuned_fine <- tune_tree(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                        order = "order_in_session", action = "code",
                        max_depth = 0L:3L, min_count = 10L,
                        prune = c(FALSE, TRUE), folds = 5L, seed = 1L)
print(as.data.frame(tuned_fine), digits = 4)
```

For the eight codes, the first-order model has the lowest held-out
perplexity (4.230), against 4.775 for the model without history: knowing
the previous move reduces the effective number of candidate next moves by
11%. Longer histories do not improve on this. The pruned depth-two and
depth-three trees come close (4.249 and 4.262), and the unpruned depth-three
tree, with an average of 144 contexts per fold, is worse (4.546).

```{r tune-coarse}
tuned_coarse <- tune_tree(ai_long, actor = "project", session = "session_id",
                          order = "order_in_session", action = "cluster",
                          max_depth = 0L:3L, min_count = 10L,
                          prune = c(FALSE, TRUE), folds = 5L, seed = 1L)
print(as.data.frame(tuned_coarse), digits = 4)
```

For the three categories, the pruned depth-three tree is selected, with a
held-out perplexity of 2.150 against 2.164 for the first-order model and
2.256 without history. History reduces the perplexity by only 5%, but the
reduction continues beyond the first move: at the coarse level, runs of
actions carry information that a single previous category does not.

The two state spaces thus describe the process differently. At the fine
level the identity of the previous move matters most, and longer histories
do not generalize to new sessions. Collapsing the codes into categories
removes much of that first-order information, because moves within the same
category lead to different next moves, while making longer runs of the same
category visible.

## Which histories predict which moves?

The fine tree is pruned with the likelihood-ratio criterion before its
contexts are read.

```{r prune}
fine_pruned <- prune_tree(fine, criterion = "G2")
fine_pruned
```

The pruned tree keeps 24 of 161 nodes. `divergent_pathways()` ranks the
retained contexts by how far their next-move distribution departs from that
of their parent context.

```{r divergent}
divergent_pathways(fine_pruned, top = 10, min_count = 20L)
```

The rare moves are the most informative contexts. An `Ask` is followed by
an `Explain` (0.48), a `Delegate` by a `Plan` (0.62) and an `Explain` by an
`Investigate` (0.31); each of these changes the predicted next move away
from `Execute`, the most likely move without history. `Investigate`, which
is frequent, is followed most often by `Plan` (0.44). Two second-order
contexts redirect the prediction of their parents: after
`Explain -> Repair` the most likely next move is another `Explain` (0.46),
whereas `Repair` alone leads to `Execute`, and after `Repair -> Investigate`
the most likely next move is `Execute` (0.47), whereas `Investigate` alone
leads to `Plan`.

`plot_pathways()` draws the next-move distribution of each context as a
heatmap.

```{r pathways-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_pathways(fine_pruned, min_count = 20L)
```

The heatmap shows the 20 most frequent contexts with at least 20
occurrences. Each row is a context and each column a next move; the cell
shows the conditional probability, and a leading `>` marks the five
contexts whose most likely next move differs from that of their parent. The
`Execute` column is dark for most contexts, which reflects the dominance of
execution in these sessions. The marked rows depart from it: `Delegate`
concentrates its probability on `Plan` (0.62), `Ask` on `Explain` (0.48),
and `Investigate` and `Repair -> Investigate` lead to `Plan` and `Execute`
respectively.

## Which histories precede a repair?

A repair move signals that something in the collaboration has to be
corrected, which makes the histories that lead to it of particular
interest. `mine_contexts()` lists, for one move, its probability after each
context of the tree. Contexts seen fewer than 30 times are dropped.

```{r mine-repair}
mine_contexts(fine_pruned, "Repair", min_count = 30L)
```

Without history, the probability of a repair is 0.030. It is highest after
`Explain -> Plan` (0.166, 30 occurrences), and it is raised after a
`Report` (0.086) and after an `Explain` (0.083), roughly three times the
baseline. Two three-move contexts, `Explain -> Investigate -> Execute`
(0.125) and `Repair -> Execute -> Execute` (0.113), show that an
explanation or a repair two moves earlier also raises the chance of a
repair. A repair directly after `Explain -> Repair` is almost never
observed (0.001, the smoothing floor). After the frequent `Execute` and `Investigate` moves it stays
close to or below the baseline (0.030 and 0.018). Repair is never the most
likely next move (`is_modal` is `FALSE` throughout): even in the contexts
that raise it, repairs remain the exception. Repairs are therefore more
likely after communication moves, explanations and reports, than after
action moves, which is consistent with repairs that follow a description of
what went wrong rather than the action itself.

The same question can be asked of the unpruned tree, which keeps contexts
that the G² test does not support. A lower probability bound restricts the
list to contexts in which a repair is at least three times as likely as
without history.

```{r mine-repair-unpruned}
mine_contexts(fine, "Repair", min_prob = 0.09, min_count = 20L)
```

The unpruned tree adds contexts such as `Ask -> Explain` (0.15) and
`Repair -> Explain` (0.14), again ending in communication moves. These
contexts are not retained by pruning, so they are candidates for further
study rather than established findings.

## What the analysis shows

The way the log is cut into sequences changes the data: because the Unix
timestamps hold only the session date, a time-gap rule merges same-day
sessions into 160 sequences, and the session column is needed to recover the
428 sessions. In the fine state space the previous move carries most of the
predictive information, and rare moves such as `Ask` and `Delegate` are the
most informative contexts; in the coarse space the effect of history is
smaller but extends over longer runs. Repairs are rare, and they are most
likely after explanations and reports.

The analysis has limits. `ai_long` is a bundled example dataset, and its
codes do not identify whether a move was made by the human or the AI
assistant, so the pathways describe the joint conversation rather than
either partner. Sessions are nested within 34 projects, and the tree pools
them; projects with many sessions weigh more heavily in every estimate. The
contexts in which repairs are more likely are based on 30 to a few hundred
occurrences, and their reliability under resampling of sessions can be
checked with `bootstrap_pathways()`.
